About This Part
Volume 8B moves from single-resource foundations to resilient Google Cloud infrastructure. The focus is not
only on creating virtual machines, networks, and storage. The focus is on building replaceable fleets, centrally
governed connectivity, health-aware application delivery, protected data, recoverable operations, and evidence-
driven production practices. Each chapter explains design intent before implementation. Labs emphasize least privilege, private
connectivity, rollback, recovery testing, cost cleanup, and the difference between availability, backup, and
disaster recovery. Volume 8 Progress

Chapter 11 - Advanced Compute Engine and Fleet Operations
Engineering virtual machines as governed, observable, replaceable infrastructure
Learning Objectives

Design VM configurations for security, performance, availability, and lifecycle management.

Use instance templates, custom images, startup automation, Shielded VM, and confidential-computing
options appropriately.

Explain maintenance behavior, Local SSD trade-offs, reservations, and spot capacity.

Operate VM fleets through policy, patching, logging, and controlled access.
11.1 From Individual VMs to Managed Fleet Standards
A production VM should be created from an approved configuration rather than assembled manually. The
standard includes machine family, image source, disk type, network tags or secure tags, service account,
Shielded VM settings, metadata, startup behavior, logging, backup policy, maintenance behavior, and
ownership labels.

Treat the boot disk as replaceable; store durable application data on managed data services or protected
data disks.

Use image families or versioned custom images with tested rollback.

Use instance templates for repeatable fleet creation.

Record business owner, environment, application, data classification, and expiry through labels or tags.
11.2 Machine Families, Scheduling, and Capacity
Machine selection is a workload decision, not a default-size decision. General-purpose families suit broad
workloads; compute-, memory-, storage-, accelerator-, and specialized families target specific bottlenecks. Capacity must also be considered by region and zone. Reservations can protect required capacity, while Spot
VMs reduce cost for interruption-tolerant workloads.

11.3 Identity, Metadata, and Administrative Access
Attach a dedicated service account with the minimum roles needed by the workload. Avoid broad OAuth scopes
and service-account keys. Use OS Login and Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding for controlled administration
when possible. Metadata and startup scripts are powerful configuration channels and must not contain
plaintext secrets.

11.4 Maintenance, Patching, and Observability
Compute Engine can live-migrate many VMs during infrastructure maintenance, but some accelerators,
specialized machine types, or Local SSD configurations can require termination behavior. Define automatic
restart, maintenance policy, patch windows, and recovery expectations. Install the Ops Agent where
appropriate and centralize logs, metrics, audit evidence, and inventory.

Use VM Manager or controlled image replacement for patch compliance.

Monitor guest health, disk pressure, startup failures, and service-account permission errors.

Prefer immutable replacement over repeated manual repair.

Validate deletion protection and disk auto-delete behavior before decommissioning.
11.5 Image and Configuration Promotion
A controlled image pipeline creates a candidate image, scans and tests it, deploys it to a nonproduction fleet,
captures health evidence, and promotes an immutable version. Emergency patching must still converge back to
the approved configuration; otherwise fleets accumulate drift. Troubleshooting Matrix

Prerequisites

A dedicated project, custom VPC/subnet, and permissions to create Compute Engine resources. Implementation
1. Create a dedicated runtime service account with one read-only role needed by the demo workload.
2. Create a startup script that installs a small web service without embedding secrets.
3. Create an instance template using a supported image family, private IP only, Shielded VM features, labels,
and the dedicated service account.
4. Launch a test VM from the template and access it through IAP or another approved private path.
5. Capture serial output, guest logs, service-account identity, disk settings, and allowed/denied API tests.

6. Create a second template version and document rollback to the first version. Validation Evidence

The VM has no public IP.

The runtime identity cannot perform an unrelated privileged action.

The application survives a controlled restart.

Template versions and rollback instructions are recorded. Cleanup

Delete the test VM and unused template versions. Verify that no orphaned disks, reservations, or static
addresses remain. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why use instance templates for VM fleets?
They provide versioned, repeatable configuration for managed instance groups and reduce manual drift.
2. When is Local SSD appropriate?
For high-performance temporary data that can be lost and reconstructed when the VM or host fails.
3. Why prefer IAP and OS Login over public SSH?
They reduce public exposure and centralize identity, authorization, and audit evidence.
4. What is immutable VM operations?
Updating a fleet by replacing instances from a tested image or template rather than repeatedly modifying
long-lived servers. Chapter Summary

Production VMs require approved identity, image, network, disk, and maintenance standards.

Private administration and short-lived identity reduce exposure.

Local SSD and Spot capacity require interruption-aware design.

Replacement-based operations limit drift and improve rollback.

Chapter 12 - Managed Instance Groups, Autoscaling, and Safe
Deployments
Building self-healing, multi-zone Compute Engine fleets with controlled change
Learning Objectives

Differentiate managed and unmanaged instance groups.

Design regional managed instance groups with health checks and autohealing.

Select autoscaling signals, initialization periods, and scale-in controls.

Use rolling and canary updates with rollback evidence.
12.1 Managed Instance Group Architecture
A managed instance group (MIG) creates and maintains VMs from an instance template. It can autoheal
unhealthy instances, autoscale, distribute instances across zones, and perform rolling or canary updates. Regional MIGs improve resilience to zonal failure by distributing capacity across multiple zones in a region. Group Type

12.2 Health Checks and Autohealing
Load-balancer health checks decide whether traffic should reach a backend. MIG autohealing health checks
decide whether a VM should be repaired or recreated. These functions can use similar probes but have different
consequences.


Probe application readiness, not only whether the operating system is running.

Set an initial delay that covers startup and dependency initialization.




12.3 Autoscaling as a Feedback System
Autoscaling can use CPU utilization, load-balancing capacity, Cloud Monitoring metrics, schedules, or queue-
based signals such as Pub/Sub for supported zonal scenarios. Stable scaling requires a signal aligned with user
demand, realistic initialization time, maximum capacity, and downstream limits. Signal

12.4 Rolling, Canary, and Opportunistic Updates
MIG updates change the intended configuration and apply it according to an update policy. Proactive rolling
updates replace instances automatically. Canary updates expose a subset of the fleet to a new template. Opportunistic policies update instances when they are otherwise recreated. Configure maximum surge and
maximum unavailable values based on capacity and risk.
gcloud compute instance-groups managed rolling-action start-update MIG_NAME \
--version=template=NEW_TEMPLATE \
--max-surge=1 --max-unavailable=0 --region=REGION
12.5 Stateful MIGs and Data Boundaries
Stateful MIGs preserve selected disks, internal IP addresses, metadata, or instance names through recreation. They can improve operations for some stateful systems, but they do not remove the need for application
replication, backup, fencing, and recovery testing. Use managed databases where they better match the
workload. Troubleshooting Matrix

Prerequisites

A versioned instance template and two or more zones in one region.

Implementation
1. Create an application health check and validate it directly.
2. Create a regional MIG with a minimum of two instances distributed across zones.
3. Configure autohealing with a realistic initial delay.
4. Attach autoscaling based on load-balancing capacity or a suitable monitoring metric.
5. Deploy a second template as a canary to a small percentage of instances.
6. Generate load, observe scaling, intentionally fail one instance, and record repair behavior.
7. Promote or roll back the canary using documented thresholds. Validation Evidence

Traffic remains available during one instance failure.

The MIG repairs the unhealthy instance.

Autoscaling changes capacity without exceeding the configured maximum.

Canary health and rollback evidence are preserved. Cleanup

Remove autoscaling and delete the MIG, templates, and health-check resources that are not required for
later labs. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. What is the difference between load-balancer health and autohealing health?
Load-balancer health controls traffic routing; autohealing health can trigger VM recreation.
2. Why use a regional MIG?
To distribute a fleet across zones and reduce the impact of a zonal outage.
3. What causes autoscaling thrash?
Noisy or lagging signals, unrealistic initialization, conflicting policies, and a narrow capacity range.
4. What should govern a rolling update?
Health evidence, surge/unavailable capacity, representative canaries, rollback criteria, quota, and
downstream capacity.

downstream capacity. Chapter Summary

MIGs deliver template-driven repair, scaling, and deployment.

Regional groups protect stateless fleets from zonal failure.

Health checks and initialization settings must reflect real application behavior.

Canary and rollback evidence are mandatory for safe fleet change.

Chapter 13 - Enterprise VPC and Shared VPC Architecture
Centralizing network governance while preserving workload autonomy
Learning Objectives

Design multi-project network boundaries using Shared VPC.

Explain host projects, service projects, subnet IAM, and delegated administration.

Plan IP ranges, routes, peering, Private Service Connect, and private services access.

Operate global VPC networks with regional failure and ownership awareness.
13.1 Global VPC, Regional Subnets, and Project Boundaries
A Google Cloud VPC network is global, while its subnets are regional. This model allows one network to span
regions, but address planning, routing, firewall policy, and service availability still require regional design. Projects are administrative boundaries; Shared VPC allows a centrally governed network in a host project to be
consumed by service projects. Component

13.2 Shared VPC Operating Model
A host project owns the Shared VPC network, subnets, routes, and network-level controls. Service projects
create resources such as VMs and GKE clusters that attach to authorized host-project subnets.

VPC Operating Model
A host project owns the Shared VPC network, subnets, routes, and network-level controls. Service projects
create resources such as VMs and GKE clusters that attach to authorized host-project subnets. Shared VPC
administrators, network administrators, security administrators, and service-project administrators should be
separate roles.

Grant Network User at the narrowest practical subnet scope.

Create Cloud NAT and shared network services in the host project.

Centralize DNS and firewall policy while preserving workload project IAM.

Use organization policy to restrict unauthorized Shared VPC patterns.
13.3 IP Address Management and Route Design
IP planning must account for primary ranges, secondary ranges, hybrid networks, service producer ranges,
future regions, mergers, and multicloud connections. Overlapping ranges block routing options and complicate
migration. Dynamic routes learned through Cloud Router are controlled by routing mode and BGP policy.

Reserve contiguous non-overlapping ranges by region and environment.

Document route ownership, next hops, priority, and propagation.

Use Connectivity Tests and route inspection before changing production paths.

The shared network, subnets, routes, and central network controls consumed by attached service projects.
2. Is a Google Cloud VPC regional?
No. The VPC is global; subnets are regional.
3. Is VPC Network Peering transitive?
No. A network cannot automatically route through one peer to reach another peer.

Chapter 14 - Network Security, Routing, NAT, and Secure
Administration
Applying layered controls to ingress, egress, lateral movement, and administration
Learning Objectives

Use hierarchical firewall policies, global/regional network firewall policies, and VPC firewall rules correctly.

Design route priority, Cloud Router, and NAT behavior.

Implement private administration through IAP, OS Login, and controlled bastion patterns.

Troubleshoot network paths using logs and Connectivity Tests.
14.1 Firewall Evaluation and Policy Hierarchy
Google Cloud supports hierarchical firewall policies at organization or folder scope, network firewall policies,
and VPC firewall rules. Policies can enforce central guardrails while workload teams manage narrower rules. Both allowed and denied traffic should be observable through logging where the risk justifies the cost. Control

14.2 Targets, Identities, and Least Privilege
Firewall rules can target resources through network tags or secure tags and, for supported cases, service
accounts. Tags must be governed because changing a tag can change network access. Use narrow source ranges,
protocol/port sets, and destination controls.

ough network tags or secure tags and, for supported cases, service
accounts. Tags must be governed because changing a tag can change network access. Use narrow source ranges,
protocol/port sets, and destination controls. Egress is part of the security boundary, not an afterthought.
14.3 Routes, Cloud Router, and Dynamic Exchange
Routes select next hops based on destination prefix, priority, applicability, and route type. Cloud Router
exchanges dynamic routes by BGP for HA VPN and Interconnect; it does not forward packets itself. Custom
route advertisements and routing mode determine which prefixes are exchanged.

Document route priority and ownership.

Avoid broad 0.0.0.0/0 custom routes without controlled next hops.

Use Network Intelligence Center and Connectivity Tests before and after route changes.

Monitor BGP session state and learned/advertised prefixes.
14.4 Public and Private Cloud NAT
Public Cloud NAT provides outbound internet connectivity for supported private resources without assigning
external IP addresses. It is regional and depends on Cloud Router configuration. Private NAT translates

addresses between private networks for supported scenarios. NAT does not replace firewall policy and does not
allow unsolicited inbound connections.

session controls. Packet Mirroring, VPC Flow Logs, firewall logs, Cloud NAT logs, and Connectivity Tests provide
complementary evidence. Troubleshooting Matrix

1. Create a Cloud Router and Public Cloud NAT for the private subnet.
2. Deploy a private VM with no external IP and a dedicated service account.



Cleanup

Delete the VM, NAT gateway, router, temporary rules, and logs sinks created only for the lab. Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Does Cloud NAT allow inbound connections?
No. It provides address translation for supported outbound flows and does not create unsolicited inbound
reachability.
2. What is Cloud Router?
A managed BGP control-plane service that exchanges dynamic routes; it does not forward data packets.
3. Why use hierarchical firewall policies?
To enforce central security guardrails across folders or the organization while allowing delegated workload
rules.
4. What evidence should support network troubleshooting?
Effective routes and firewall policies, Connectivity Tests, flow/firewall/NAT logs, DNS results, and BGP state. Chapter Summary

Network security is layered across hierarchy, VPC, edge, routes, and identity.

20.1 Availability Is Not Backup
A multi-zone application can remain available during infrastructure failure, but it can still replicate accidental
deletion, corruption, or malicious change. Backup preserves recoverable history. Replication reduces data loss
or recovery time for selected failures. Disaster recovery coordinates people, infrastructure, data, identity, DNS,
dependencies, and communications after a major event. Capability

20.2 RTO, RPO, and Recovery Tiers
Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable outage duration. Recovery point objective (RPO) is
the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time. Smaller objectives usually require more replication,

20.3 Google Cloud Data-Protection Building Blocks
Disk snapshot schedules automate incremental protection for Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk. Regional disks and
Hyperdisk HA provide synchronous zonal replication for supported workloads. Asynchronous disk replication
supports selected cross-region scenarios. Cloud Storage offers soft delete, versioning, lifecycle, retention, and
location choices. Filestore provides backups and restore. Managed databases have service-specific backup and
replication controls covered in Part C.
20.4 Backup and DR Service
Backup and DR Service provides centralized, policy-based backup management, monitoring, reporting, and
recovery for supported workloads. Backup vaults can provide immutable, indelible backup storage to improve
cyber resilience. Compute Engine backup plans can protect instance data, and application-consistent
capabilities can coordinate pre/post scripts for supported workflows. Always verify current support, frequency,
location, and restore constraints.





Monitor job success, age of last recovery point, retention compliance, and restore test outcomes.

Do not treat a successful backup job as proof of recoverability.
20.5 Disaster-Recovery Architecture Patterns
Patterns include backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active-active. Choose based on RTO/RPO,
data consistency, cost, operations maturity, and regulatory location.

Patterns include backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active-active. Choose based on RTO/RPO,
data consistency, cost, operations maturity, and regulatory location. Infrastructure as Code, versioned images,

20.6 Capstone Architecture
The capstone is a private, multi-zone Compute Engine service behind a protected global Application Load
Balancer. A regional MIG supplies replaceable capacity. Cloud Storage stores protected application artifacts and
logs. Persistent Disk or a managed data layer has scheduled protection. Shared VPC-style controls, Cloud NAT,
private administration, DNS, monitoring, and a documented regional recovery path complete the design. Users -> Global Application Load Balancer + Cloud Armor + CDN

20.7 Recovery Game Day
A game day declares a scenario, freezes unrelated changes, captures baseline health, executes failure or restore
steps, measures RTO/RPO, validates data and security, and records gaps. The exercise should include one failed
restore or missing dependency to test diagnosis and decision-making, not only the happy path.
